title: Restriction of scalars and linearized functors
statement:
Let $S\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ be a strong monoidal functor and $P\colon\mathcal C\to
\mathcal D$ a functor with a projection formula $P(SL\otimes M)\cong L\otimes PM$, so that $P$
linearizes to $P_B\colon\Mod_{SB}(\mathcal C)\to\Mod_B(\mathcal D)$ for every monoid object $B$
of $\mathcal D$ ([sk-def-sfb-transport]). For a morphism of monoid objects
$\varphi\colon B\to B'$ there is a natural isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{Res}_\varphi\circ P_{B'}\;\cong\;P_B\circ\operatorname{Res}_{S\varphi}\colon
\Mod_{SB'}(\mathcal C)\longrightarrow\Mod_B(\mathcal D),
$$

the identity on underlying objects.

proof.text:
Put $F=\operatorname{Res}_\varphi\circ P_{B'}$ and $G=P_B\circ\operatorname{Res}_{S\varphi}$. By clause 1 of [det-def-sfb-ring-object-transport], the strong monoidal functor $S$ transports $B,B'$ to monoids $SB,SB'$ and transports $\varphi$ to a monoid morphism $S\varphi$. Thus both restrictions are defined. For an $SB'$-module $M$ with action $\gamma_M\colon SB'\otimes M\to M$, [def-sfb-modobj-linearization] and [def-sfb-modobj-restriction] give the common underlying object $PM$ and the respective $B$-actions
$$a_F=P\gamma_M\circ\pi^{-1}_{B',M}\circ(\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_{PM}),\qquad a_G=P\bigl(\gamma_M\circ(S\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\bigr)\circ\pi^{-1}_{B,M}.$$
Here $\pi$ is the projection formula of the statement. The functors on both sides exist by the cited linearization and restriction constructions; no colimits, closedness, braiding or commutativity of the monoids are required.

source.place: first two sentences: compute the two actions

proof.text:
Naturality in $L$ in [def-sfb-projection-formula], applied to $\varphi\colon B\to B'$ at the underlying object $M$, is
$$\pi_{B',M}\circ P(S\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)=(\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_{PM})\circ\pi_{B,M}.$$
Compose on the left with $\pi^{-1}_{B',M}$ and on the right with $\pi^{-1}_{B,M}$. Cancellation of each isomorphism gives
$$\pi^{-1}_{B',M}\circ(\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_{PM})=P(S\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\pi^{-1}_{B,M}.$$
Postcompose with $P\gamma_M$ and use $P\gamma_M\circ P(S\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)=P\bigl(\gamma_M\circ(S\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\bigr)$ by functoriality. Substitution in step 1 proves $a_F=a_G$.

source.place: last sentence: equality of actions by naturality in L

proof.text: The morphism condition of [sk-def-sfb-module-objects] says that $h\colon(PM,a_F)\to(PM,a_G)$ is $B$-linear exactly when $h\circ a_F=a_G\circ(\mathrm{id}_B\otimes h)$. For $h=\mathrm{id}_{PM}$ this is precisely the equality $a_F=a_G$ proved in step 2. Define $\eta_M\colon F(M)\to G(M)$ by this identity map. The reverse identity is also $B$-linear, since $a_G=a_F$, and is inverse to $\eta_M$: both composites have underlying identity, and module morphisms have the underlying composition by the same definition. Hence $\eta_M$ is an isomorphism, with identity underlying map in both directions.

source.place: last sentence: identity of PM is a module morphism; explicit inverse

proof.text: For an $SB'$-linear morphism $f\colon M\to N$, restriction leaves the underlying morphism fixed by [def-sfb-modobj-restriction], and linearization sends it to $Pf$ by [def-sfb-modobj-linearization]. Therefore $F(f)$ and $G(f)$ both have underlying morphism $Pf$. The two sides of $G(f)\circ\eta_M=\eta_N\circ F(f)$ have underlying morphisms $Pf\circ\mathrm{id}_{PM}$ and $\mathrm{id}_{PN}\circ Pf$, respectively, both equal to $Pf$. Module morphisms in [sk-def-sfb-module-objects] are underlying morphisms satisfying an equation, so this equality proves naturality. Write $\theta_M=\eta_M^{-1}$ for the reverse identity module map constructed in step 3. The underlying maps of $F(f)\circ\theta_M$ and $\theta_N\circ G(f)$ are respectively $Pf\circ\mathrm{id}_{PM}$ and $\mathrm{id}_{PN}\circ Pf$, both equal to $Pf$; equality of underlying module arrows gives $F(f)\circ\theta_M=\theta_N\circ G(f)$, proving naturality of the inverse. Together with step 3 they define the required natural isomorphism $F\cong G$, the identity on underlying objects.

source.place: last sentence: natural in M, including naturality of the inverse
